name: create_image_pro_flash
description:
Create one Pro Flash pixel-art image with an optional left-box style image.

Custom sizes (Beta) accept width and height from 16 to 256 in multiples of 4 pixels.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for native presets and provisional cost.
The style image accepts {url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}; prefer URLs
for uploaded images. Style art must fit the native canvas without resizing.
style_options selects color_palette, outline, detail and shading independently.
Default style uses existing PixelLab art. Returns one image; the provisional
generation charge varies with the canvas. Failed pixel grids use image-to-
pixel-art with fixer on the generated box. Poll get_image(job_id); use
source_image_id after completion.

width.description: Native sizes: 16x16 (experimental), 24x24, 32x32, 32x48, 48x48, 64x64, 96x64, 96x96, 128x128. Custom size (Beta): integer width 16–256 and height 16–256. Both dimensions must be multiples of 4 pixels. Pixel-grid recovery uses image-to-pixel-art with fixer when needed. No native image resizing.

style_image.description: One URL, encoded image, or owned image ID plus its reference instructions.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

style_options.description: Choose which visual traits to copy from the style image.

name: edit_image_pro_flash
description:
Edit one Pro Flash image at its unchanged native canvas size.

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
method=text requires description; method=reference requires reference_image
({url}, {base64}, or {source_image_id}). References must fit the source canvas.
No-background defaults to the source's transparency. Optional palette
correction matches source colors. Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for exact
shapes. Returns one queued image; poll get_image(job_id), then download.

reference_image.description: One URL, encoded image, or owned image ID plus its reference instructions.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

name: inpaint_image_pro_flash
description:
Replace white-mask pixels with Pro Flash, preserving unmasked RGBA bytes exactly.

Source: image_url, image_base64, or owned source_image_id. Mask: a rectangle
(all four mask_x/y/width/height), OR a same-size mask PNG via base64/URL.
Mask RGB must be pure white=generate or black=keep; mask alpha is ignored.
Empty masks are rejected. crop_to_mask is always true. Changes-only output
is transparent outside the mask; Modify current layer returns a composite.
Optional context_image requires bounding_box locating the source and is at
most three times its native dimensions. No images or masks are rescaled.
Query get_pro_flash_capabilities for shapes; poll the job with get_image.

context_image.description: One URL, encoded image, or owned image ID plus its reference instructions.

usage_description.description: How this reference should guide appearance.

bounding_box.description: The native source rectangle within the additional context image.

name: create_image_pixen
description:
Generate a freeform pixel-art image with the Pixen model.

Pixen is the newer of the two fast generators and holds up better on small
sprites. Pick between the three text-to-image tools like this:
- create_image_pixflux — when you need an init image (img2img), a palette
  given as an image, isometric, or shading control.
- create_image_pixen — this one; cleaner small sprites, bigger canvas.
- create_image_pro — best quality, returns a set of candidates, costs more;
  takes a palette as hex colours (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, NES, Lospec).

Canvas: 16-768 per side and each side must be a multiple of 4; total area
16x16 to 512x512. Below 32 the canvas must be SQUARE, so the small sizes
are 16x16, 20x20, 24x24 and 28x28.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~10-40 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'ornate iron key', 'mossy stone wall').

width.description: Canvas width in pixels. Must be a multiple of 4; width must equal height when either side is below 32. width x height may not exceed 512x512 = 262,144, so the widest canvases are e.g. 768x340 or 680x384, not 768x384.

height.description: Canvas height in pixels. Must be a multiple of 4; height must equal width when either side is below 32.

no_background.description: Return the subject on a transparent background. True for sprites and items, False for scenes.

direction.description: Which way the subject faces (weakly guiding).

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

name: create_image_pro
description:
Generate pixel art with the Pro model — best quality, several candidates.

This is "Create Image (Pro)". It returns a SET of options in one call rather
than a single image, by the larger side: 64 candidates up to 32px, 49 at
33-35px, 36 at 36-41px, 25 at 42-50px, 16 at 51-64px, 9 at 65-84px, 16 at
85px, 4 at 86-170px, 1 above that. Cost is per call, not per candidate, so a
small canvas is where it pays off.

Unlike the other two text-to-image tools it accepts labelled references:
  create_image_pro(
      description="knight in the same armour",
      reference_images='[{"base64": "<hero png>", "usage": "character base"},
                         {"base64": "<armour png>", "usage": "outfit"}]')

No facing control: nothing here sets which way the subject looks, and a
reference does not either. To turn a picture you already have into 8
facings, use create_object_pro_flash(first_frame_base64=..., n_directions=8).

For a console or palette look (1-bit, Game Boy, PICO-8, NES, any palette from
Lospec) pass `palette` as its hex colours, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856",
"#88c070", "#e0f8d0"], plus `palette_name`: the image is drawn for the
palette and comes back using only those colours. A palette name alone is not
enough - the colours are what the result is put on. `max_colors` caps the
colours in each image (e.g. 6 for an NES-style sprite).

Pick between the three: create_image_pixflux for img2img or isometric;
create_image_pixen for clean small sprites at 1 generation; this one when
quality matters more than cost, or for a palette given as hex colours.

Cost: 10-25 generations. Generation time: ~1-10 minutes (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

description.description: What to draw (e.g. 'ornate iron key with a ruby inlay').

width.description: Canvas width. Max depends on aspect ratio (512x512 square, 688x384 for 16:9).

height.description: Canvas height. Max depends on aspect ratio.

no_background.description: Return subjects on a transparent background. Defaults True — pro is normally used for assets. Set False for scenes and backdrops.

reference_images.description: Up to 4 LABELLED reference images, as a JSON array. Each entry takes a "url" (preferred) OR a "base64": [{"url": "https://...", "usage": "character base"}, {"url": "https://...", "usage": "outfit and armour"}]. The "usage" note tells the model what to take from each image, which is what makes combining several references work. Prefer urls here especially — four inline images in one argument is four times the payload, and MCP clients truncate large arguments. Sizes are read from the images.

style_image_base64.description: One image whose art style (palette, outline, detail, shading) the result should match. Use style_copy to narrow which of those apply.

style_image_url.description: Alternative to style_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the style PNG. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

style_copy.description: Which aspects to take from style_image_base64: any of color_palette, outline, detail, shading. Defaults to all four, or all but color_palette when a palette is given.

palette.description: Target palette, 2 to 256 hex colours as a JSON array, e.g. ["#081820", "#346856", "#88c070", "#e0f8d0"] for Game Boy or ["#000000", "#ffffff"] for 1-bit. The image is drawn for these colours and every pixel of the result is one of them.

palette_name.description: Optional name of the palette (e.g. 'Game Boy', 'PICO-8', 'NES'); naming it helps the look.

max_colors.description: At most this many colours in each image (2-64), e.g. 6 for an NES-style sprite. With a palette, they are picked from it.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

name: list_images
description:
List the images in your Creator gallery (pixellab.ai/create), newest first,
one line each: its `gallery:<id>` reference, description, size and frame
count. Use the reference with pixelart_workbench to look at or edit an image,
and with save_to_asset to save a fix over it.

limit.description: Maximum number of images to return

search.description: Filter by the description an image was made from, or its id, case-insensitive. 'knight' finds 'armored knight with a sword'.

name: image_to_pixelart
description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art.

This is the general-purpose converter: give it any picture and get pixel art
back at the size you ask for. Use it when a user brings their own artwork,
a screenshot, or an AI render and wants it as a sprite.

Two dials decide how much licence the model takes:
- default (faithful=False, init_image_strength=0) — reinterprets the subject
  as pixel art. Cleanest sprites, least like the original.
- faithful=True with init_image_strength around 100-300 — reproduces the
  source. Use it when the user says "keep it exactly like this". Higher is
  NOT more faithful in a useful way: past ~300 the model stops transforming
  and returns the source image, which is not pixel art.

Related tools: create_portrait_character converts a picture into a character
portrait specifically; unzoom_image is what you want if the input is ALREADY
pixel art that has merely been upscaled — running it through here would
redraw art that only needed downscaling.

Input max area 2048x2048, output max 512x512.

Cost: 1 generation. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the image to convert. Any artwork, render or photo. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the source image. PREFER THIS for anything but a tiny sprite. Give one, not both.

output_width.description: Width of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source width. Keep the source's aspect ratio.

output_height.description: Height of the pixel art result. Defaults to a quarter of the source height.

faithful.description: Faithful mode. Stays true to the source instead of reinterpreting it as pixel art. Turn this on when the user wants THEIR artwork converted rather than a pixel-art take on it; pair it with a init_image_strength of 100-300.

init_image_strength.description: How strongly to start from the source image (img2img). 0 redraws from scratch using the source only as guidance; 100-300 keeps its composition and colors. Do NOT go higher to be 'more faithful' — past ~300 the model barely transforms the input and hands back the source rather than pixel art.

text_guidance_scale.description: How hard to push towards pixel-art style.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

name: image_to_pixelart_pro_flash
description:
Convert an image, render or photo into pixel art with Pro Flash.

Redraws the picture as clean pixel art and picks the output size itself
(detected pixel scale), so there is no size parameter. Use image_to_pixelart
instead when the result must be an exact width and height. Optional
description steers the style (palette, dithering, mood).

Supply image_url (preferred), image_base64, or an owned source_image_id.
Sources over 2048px on the longest side are scaled down first. Transparent
areas become a white background.

Cost: 6 generations. ~30-60 seconds. Returns one queued image; poll
get_image(job_id), then download.

name: unzoom_image
description:
Downscale upscaled pixel art back onto its true pixel grid.

Pixel art found online is almost always scaled up — a 32x32 sprite saved at
512x512, where every art pixel is a 16x16 block. Every tool that takes a
reference or style image works far better on the real 32x32 sprite, and this
recovers it: the pixel grid is detected and the image is downsampled onto it.

Run this FIRST whenever a user supplies pixel art from outside PixelLab and
you are about to pass it to create_image_pixflux(init_image), a style image,
edit_image, or create_character. If the art was never upscaled it is already
at native size and this is unnecessary.

Do not confuse it with image_to_pixelart: that CONVERTS a non-pixel-art
picture, redrawing it. This one only downscales art that is already pixel art.

Input must be at least 256x256 (grid detection needs the pixels) and at most
2048x2048 in area.

The result is OPAQUE: grid detection works in RGB, so transparency in the
input is composited onto white first. If the user needs a cut-out sprite
back, tell them so rather than handing back a white-boxed result.

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in under a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

image_base64.description: Base64 PNG/JPEG of the upscaled pixel art. PREFER image_url — MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64, and unzoom inputs are big by definition.

image_url.description: Alternative to image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the upscaled image. PREFER THIS. Give one, not both.

quantize.description: Palette handling for the result. 0 auto-detects a palette, -1 keeps every color the downsample produces, 2-256 quantizes to exactly that many colors.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

name: correct_pixelart
description:
Clean up pixel art — sharpen edges, drop stray pixels, tighten the palette.

Keeps the sprite on its existing pixel grid and at its existing size. Use it
on art that has been through a lossy pipeline, on hand-drawn art that needs
tidying, or on output from another tool that is nearly-but-not-quite on-grid.

Passing several frames in one call corrects them together, which is what you
want for an animation or a character's directions.

This does NOT resize. If each art pixel is a block of screen pixels the image
is upscaled, not damaged — run unzoom_image first, then correct if it still
needs it.

Transparency survives: the alpha channel is carried around the model and
re-applied, so a cutout sprite does not come back on a white box.

Max area 1024x1024 per frame.

Cost: 0.1 generations. Generation time: ~20-60 seconds (async).
Poll with get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to clean up — pass a one-element list for a single image. All frames must be the same size. PREFER image_urls; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s), one per frame. PREFER THIS. Give urls OR base64, not both.

strength.description: How far the model may move from the art. 0.1 tidies stray pixels and edges; high values redraw more and can change details. Start low and only raise it if the art needs real repair.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

name: reduce_colors
description:
Quantize images onto a smaller, shared palette.

Pixel art reads as pixel art partly because of its restricted palette. AI
output and converted artwork often carry hundreds of near-identical colors;
this snaps them onto a tight palette, optionally with ordered dithering.

Passing several frames in one call is the point: they are quantized TOGETHER,
so an animation or a character's eight directions come back sharing ONE
palette instead of drifting apart frame by frame. Quantizing them one at a
time is the mistake this tool exists to prevent.

Three ways to choose the palette:
- omit num_colors and the palette image — the size is auto-detected
- num_colors — quantize to exactly this many colors
- palette_image — reuse the colors of an existing image (the game's palette)

The result carries a `palette` strip you can feed back as palette_image_base64
to lock later frames onto the same colors.

Total size limit across all frames is 512x512 worth of pixels (sixteen 64x64
frames, or four 128x128).

Cost: 0.1 generations. Runs locally in about a second — poll once with
get_image(job_id).

images_base64.description: Base64 PNG(s) to quantize — pass a one-element list for a single image. All frames must be the same size. PREFER image_urls; MCP clients routinely truncate large inline base64.

image_urls.description: Alternative to images_base64: https, data: or `upload:<id>` (POST /v2/uploads with this same bearer token) URLs to the PNG(s), one per frame. PREFER THIS. Give urls OR base64, not both.

num_colors.description: Target number of colors. Omit to auto-detect a good palette size from the images. Cannot be combined with a palette image.

palette_image_base64.description: Base64 PNG whose colors become the palette (max 256 colors) — use it to force frames onto an existing game palette. Cannot be combined with num_colors.

palette_image_url.description: Alternative to palette_image_base64: an https (or data:) URL to the palette image. Give one, not both.

dithering.description: Ordered dithering matrix size. Larger matrices give smoother gradients at the cost of a busier look.

dithering_strength.description: How strongly to dither. Ignored when dithering is 'none'.

project_id.description: Internal Game Builder project context; the finished image is linked after generation.

name: pixelart_workbench
description:
Run one pixel-art command on a drawing or image you already made. This is
the engine's own command line: it checks work, explains it and improves it.

Check and explain (read-only):
- lint <id> [--rules outline_gap,orphan_pixel,…] — pixel-art defects, each
  naming the node and command that drew them
- inspect <id> --region x0,y0,x1,y1 --scale 10 — a zoomed crop with its
  exact colours
- measure <id> --at x,y — what is at a pixel and who drew it
- explain <id> — resolved geometry, per-command footprints, before rendering
- motion / storyboard / silhouette / reveal / clusters / parts <id> — reports
- score <id> — a 0-100 pixel-art discipline score with a breakdown
- compare <id> <id> — two results side by side

Improve (returns a NEW drawing id):
- shade <id> --band 2 --light=-1,-1 — banded shading along a colour ramp
- selout <id> — selective outlining; reoutline / clean-lines / aa / mirror
- cluster <id> --at x,y --action recolor --color <name> — one guarded cluster
- repair <id> — deterministic cleanup of drift, strays, fringe and noise

Craft operations need colour ramps: run `extract-palette <id>` first, then
pass `--ramps skin=dark,mid,light`. Anything unclear: `describe cli`,
`describe lint_rules`, `describe ramps`. Free for subscribers.

argv.description: One command line, e.g. 'lint <drawing_id> --rules outline_gap' or ['edit', '<id>', '--changes', '[…]']. Omit it for the playbook. A subject is an id or an image reference (`character:<id>:south`, a data URL, an https link) — never a file path; the server writes the output and returns a new id. Start with 'describe cli' for the full command list.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

name: vfx_workbench
description:
Make an animated pixel-art effect (spell, hit, explosion, aura, projectile,
weather...) yourself, around the user's sprite or on its own: drop in tuned
parts, write layers, look at every render, then export. Export saves it to the
user's My effects on pixellab.ai (re-editable there with sliders) and returns a
GIF and a spritesheet PNG + JSON; --game-pack adds a ZIP of every piece for a game
engine (--part <id> just one). Free for subscribers.

- start [--sprite <image>] [--projectile <image>] [--preset <name>] -> step id
- <step id> <tool> '<JSON>' -> add_part, set_part, remove_part, throw, render,
  get_preset, get_part, list_parts; a change returns a new step id
- <step id> export [--name N] [--replace <effect id>] [--game-pack | --part <id>]
- describe start | parts | recipe | craft | cookbook | edits | presets | tools

Sprites and exports are pixelart_workbench ids, so the two work together.
Start with describe start.

argv.description: One command, e.g. ['start', '--sprite', 'character:<id>:south'], ['<step id>', 'add_part', '{"name": "fire_burst"}'] or ['<step id>', 'export', '--name', 'Fireball']. Omit it for the guide.

mode.description: low (default): act directly, fewest tokens — one decisive image per result. high: think openly — fuller evidence and a review checklist; write your plan and observations in `notes`. Use the mode the user asked for.

notes.description: What you observed and what this step should achieve, in a few sentences (high mode: always; low: optional). On the first call, include the user's request. Stored with the step to improve these tools.

name: save_to_asset
description:
Save pixel art into one of your characters, objects or Creator gallery
images, replacing a rotation, one direction of an animation or a gallery
image — or add it to the gallery as a new image (free, no generation).

Use it to keep a fix made with pixelart_workbench or another image tool: the
character and object creators, the Creator gallery, downloads and game
projects then show the new pixels. The image must match what it replaces —
the same canvas size and the same number of frames; a different size can go
to the gallery as a new image. Save each direction with its own call. The
replaced frames are kept: the reply gives the save_to_asset call that puts
them back.

Examples:
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:south")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="character:<id>:east:<group id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="object:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:<id>")
- save_to_asset(image="<workbench id>", target="gallery:new",
  description="knight holding a sword, idle")

image.description: What to save: a pixelart_workbench result id (`<id>`, or `<id>:<view>` for a drawing), `job:<id>` / `job:<id>:<index>` (an image tool result), `upload:<id>` (an image POSTed to /v2/uploads), an https or data URL of a PNG or GIF, or base64.

target.description: Where to save it. A rotation: `character:<id>:<direction>`, `object:<id>:<direction>`, or `object:<id>` for a one-direction object. One direction of an animation: the same with `:<group id>` added (get_character / get_object show each animation's [group: …] id). A Creator gallery image: `gallery:<id>` to replace it (list_images shows each image's reference), `gallery:new` to add the image as a new one.

description.description: Only with target="gallery:new": what the image shows, kept as its gallery description so the website and list_images(search=...) can find it.
